questions.topic: Partitioning Strategy: Pruning What You Do Not Read
questions.question: What is the main performance goal of partitioning?
options: Skip large regions of data that cannot possibly match a query's filter
Compress each partition with a dictionary shared across the table
Guarantee that every partition holds an identical number of rows
Replace row-group statistics so the footer stays cheap to parse

questions.topic: Partitioning Strategy: Pruning What You Do Not Read
questions.question: What makes a strong partition key?
options: It holds a value distinct for almost every row in the table's history
It appears often in selective query filters and has moderate cardinality
It is derived from a hash of the row's full contents at write time
It changes value whenever an ingestion attempt is retried or replayed later

questions.topic: Partitioning Strategy: Pruning What You Do Not Read
questions.question: A 3.65-terabyte table has 365 equal daily partitions. Approximately how much data does one pruned day contain?
options: 1 gigabyte
100 gigabytes
10 gigabytes
365 gigabytes

questions.topic: Partitioning Strategy: Pruning What You Do Not Read
questions.question: Why is direct partitioning by a nearly unique user ID risky?
options: It blocks the optimizer from translating any user filter into partition pruning
It forces every user's rows into a single oversized partition directory
It strips minimum and maximum statistics from each partition's footer
It creates millions of tiny partitions whose planning cost exceeds the scan

questions.topic: Partitioning Strategy: Pruning What You Do Not Read
questions.question: What is a good alternative to one partition per high-cardinality key?
options: Bucketing the key by a hash into a fixed number of partitions
Creating one separate table per key value inside the same catalog
Storing the key as a nested field so partitioning applies per row
Raising the row group size so each partition holds a single group

questions.topic: Partitioning Strategy: Pruning What You Do Not Read
questions.question: How should engineers verify that partition pruning actually occurred?
options: Confirm the table declaration lists a partition column for the filter
Read the query plan and compare partitions or bytes actually scanned
Count how many output columns the projection finally returned to the client
Check that the partition directories were listed at least once during planning

questions.question: What makes many small analytical files inefficient?
options: Small files cannot hold a valid Parquet footer or column statistics
Small files lose rows whenever the scheduler retries a failed task
Fixed per-file listing, open, scheduling and decode costs come to dominate
Small files force every engine to read them in strict sequential order

questions.question: Which workload commonly creates small files?
options: A nightly batch job that writes each partition with a single large writer
A dashboard that reads a compacted table without writing anything
A cold partition rewritten once a quarter into large sorted files
Streaming micro-batches flushed every minute by many parallel writers

questions.question: Why can ten 1-gigabyte files outperform ten thousand 1-megabyte files containing similar total bytes?
options: Per-object and per-task overhead is amortized over far more useful bytes
Large files compress better because a codec sees the whole table at once
Large files reduce the number of row groups, which raises scan parallelism
Large files skip footer parsing entirely because their schema is inferred once

questions.question: How is file size different from Parquet row-group size?
options: Row groups are chosen by the reader, while file size is fixed at write time
One file can hold several row groups, each of which readers skip independently
Row group size is a catalog setting, while file size is a writer setting
Row groups live in the catalog, while files live in the storage bucket

questions.question: Two hundred workers each emit one file per minute. How many files can they create in one day?
Why is blindly concatenating Parquet object bytes not valid compaction?
options: Object stores refuse to serve any object assembled from more than one upload
Concatenation reorders rows, so the partition values no longer line up correctly
Concatenated bytes lose their compression codec and must be entirely re-encoded
Each file carries its own footer, so a format-aware rewrite is required

questions.topic: Compaction: Merging Files Without Breaking Readers
questions.question: What does compaction normally do?
options: Rewrites many small immutable files into fewer larger ones
Edits each source object in place to append the next batch
Deletes every retained snapshot once the newest one commits
Reassigns partition values so the data spreads more evenly

questions.topic: Compaction: Merging Files Without Breaking Readers
questions.question: What makes a compaction switch safe for concurrent readers?
options: Deleting the input files as soon as their replacements are written
An atomic metadata commit that swaps the whole old file set for the new
Reusing the input object names so readers need no metadata change
Listing the bucket after each write so readers observe the newest set

questions.question: About how many 512-megabyte outputs replace 1000 files of 8 megabytes each?

questions.topic: Compaction: Merging Files Without Breaking Readers
questions.question: Why must old input files survive beyond the commit?
options: The new snapshot still lists them alongside the compacted outputs
Compaction outputs are written lazily and contain no rows until read
Table formats cannot remove a file reference once metadata has published it
Readers and retained snapshots may still resolve to the old generation

questions.topic: Compaction: Merging Files Without Breaking Readers
questions.question: A concurrent writer changes files selected by a compactor after planning. What should optimistic concurrency do?
options: Reject the conflicting commit and force the compactor to retry or replan
Delete the other writer's newer files so the compaction snapshot stays valid
Commit both file sets and let readers deduplicate the overlapping rows
Rewrite the bucket listing so the newest objects appear to be inputs

questions.topic: Compaction: Merging Files Without Breaking Readers
questions.question: A compactor crashes after writing outputs but before metadata commit. How should those files be treated?
options: As table data that the next reader will discover through a prefix listing
As unreferenced orphans that a delayed cleanup job may safely remove
As the authoritative replacement for every file in that partition
As evidence that the compare-and-swap commit already succeeded once
